newsitem.title: PERU: Rebels turn up pressure on Peru, Japan before talks.
newsitem.headline: Rebels turn up pressure on Peru, Japan before talks.

text.p: The rebel group holding hostages in Lima piled pressure on Peruvian and Japanese leaders on Friday before their weekend summit, warning that both nations would share the blame if a peaceful solution were not found to the 45-day-long crisis.
"We have patience, serenity and all the time in the world to reach a political agreement," said the international spokesman for the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), Isaac Velazco.
"We are used to this type of situation. The others (hostages) inside are not," he told Reuters in an interview from Hamburg.
"The Japanese government will be responsible as well if this is not resolved (peacefully) because it is backing Fujimori's moves," he added.
Velazco urged Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto to convince Peru's President Alberto Fujimori during a meeting on Saturday in Toronto to seek a quick political solution.

He said Fujimori was playing a dangerous game by suggesting he could wait weeks or even months rather than give in to the rebels' demand to free 400 jailed comrades in return for the release of the 72 VIP hostages.
Fujimori and Hashimoto were set to meet in Toronto to agree on a strategy over how to handle the 45-day-old siege in the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima.

A Japanese government source said Tokyo and Lima were divided over whether the time had come to give ground on the rebels' main demand that Peru free jailed guerrillas. Fujimori has refused to discuss this condition.

"We are worried that there could be an unexpected development. Direct negotiations must be held soon," the Tokyo source said. Hashimoto, he said, would urge Fujimori to soften his position to allow the rebels' demand on the talks agenda.
Tokyo also criticised Peru for endangering the lives of hostages -- including about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen -- with its bold police tactics at the site.
Hashimoto, who left Tokyo on Friday, called several times this week for Fujimori to exercise caution to prevent "accidents or incidents."
Before leaving for Toronto, Fujimori sought to defuse tensions between the two governments by saying that stricter orders to police officers were needed.
He told Argentina's CVN television network obscene gestures by police that provoked the rebels earlier this week to fire several shots at the officers "were not planned."
However, a senior Peruvian government source, speaking on condition of anonymity, insisted Fujimori would not apologise to Hashimoto for the provocative police moves.

The summit, which could be preceded by an informal meeting, was aimed at achieving "a very close coordination," according to Fujimori. "If we were in an emergency situation we would need to be in close contact," he said.
But Fujimori would not use the meeting to seek approval for a military assault on the mined and booby-trapped compound, the Peruvian government source said.
Hashimoto said on Thursday the summit would confirm Tokyo and Lima's joint strategy of not "caving in to terrorism."

Fujimori said he was prepared for the six-week-old siege to drag on. "It could go on a lot longer still. I am patient (to wait) for the hostages to be freed safe and sound ... It could take some weeks, some months," Fujimori said. He added in an interview with the daily Clarin of Buenos Aires: "Remember that there was a seizure in Iran that lasted 444 days."
Before leaving for Canada, the Peruvian president also reiterated his offer to allow the guerrillas to leave Peru if a third country granted them asylum as part of a deal to end the siege.
However, the MRTA spokesman said on Friday, "We did not enter to have passage to and asylum in another country."

On Friday, police repeated tactics aimed at wearing down the rebels by blasting in the early hours broadcasts of martial music, sirens and the roar of aircraft at the building. Just before dawn they played a reveille. A twin-engine military plane also flew slowly over the site.

The MRTA rebels seized hundreds of guests when they stormed the residence on Dec. 17 during a diplomatic reception. They released most of the captives but kept those they considered the most important bargaining chips, including Fujimori's brother, top government and security force officials, two ambassadors, and the Japanese.
